subject: humanities
passage: Russian speakers must distinguish between two basic color terms, goluboy for lighter blues and siniy for darker ones, where English speakers use only "blue." In experiments, Russian speakers are faster than English speakers at telling apart two shades that fall on opposite sides of the goluboy-siniy boundary. Linguist Alina Petrova takes this as evidence that the language one speaks reshapes perception itself, so that Russian speakers literally see a sharper division among blues.
passage_b: Studies of this effect contain a revealing detail. When Russian speakers perform the same color task while silently rehearsing a string of numbers, a task that occupies verbal memory, their advantage at the goluboy-siniy boundary disappears; a demanding visual task of similar difficulty does not erase it. Language, these results suggest, speeds discrimination by being called on in the moment, as speakers covertly name what they see, rather than by permanently changing what their eyes deliver.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the interpretation offered by Petrova in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that Russian speakers are faster than English speakers at telling the shades apart
choices.B: By arguing that the advantage reflects visual training rather than knowledge of Russian
choices.C: By claiming that language has no influence on how quickly speakers tell colors apart
choices.D: By accepting the advantage but tracing it to naming in the moment, not altered perception

explanation.why: Text 2 does not question that Russian speakers have an advantage; it notes that the advantage "disappears" when verbal memory is occupied but not when a visual task is added. It concludes that language helps "by being called on in the moment ... rather than by permanently changing what their eyes deliver." Text 2 accepts the finding but rejects Petrova's claim that perception itself is reshaped.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 refers to "their advantage" as a real result; it questions only what causes it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 links the advantage to verbal naming, and a visual task does not erase it, so visual training is not its explanation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says language "speeds discrimination," so it does not deny language any influence.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 accepts the faster discrimination but explains it as silent naming during the task rather than a lasting change in what speakers see.
